A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research despite the title and method renaming, and all supplied pages are readable. However, v1 includes Appendices A–C and the reward prompt template, whereas v2 ends at the references while referring to unavailable supplementary implementation details and analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original VBench evaluations, reward-stage ablations, reward-model bias analyses, and qualitative comparisons, including additional experiments in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and ablation results, comparative training diagnostics, hyperparameter sensitivity results, and a human evaluation.

M1.justification: The reward-mixture and GRPO optimization structure remains, but its weighting rule changes beyond renaming. v1 uses beta[S(r_(j-1)) − S(r_j)], whereas v2 Eq. 6 uses beta[S(r_j) − S(r_(j+1))] and specifies the final-component boundary. v2 also drops the explicit softmax sharpness parameter alpha. These are localized revisions to the reported algorithm.

E1.justification: Both retain the DanceGRPO 50k training data, iStock prompts and videos, VBench, and text-to-video generation coverage. Generated-video bias evaluation already appears in v1 Appendix B. The new human ratings and sensitivity experiments change evaluation procedures without establishing a new generation task or data domain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds DanceGRPO with Qwen2.5-VL-72B alongside its existing VideoAlign configuration, enabling a matched-evaluator comparison. The ablation comparator set is revised and no longer includes the one-stage row. The displayed bias comparison also omits VisionReward and VideoScore, which appeared in v1 Appendix B.

E3.justification: The reported Wan-1.3B training budget increases from 150 to 220 steps; the other backbone budgets and main inference settings remain. v2 introduces two-component adaptive-versus-fixed controls, explicit tau/beta sweeps, and a five-level human comparison involving 65 raters evaluating 20 video pairs each. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds reward-conflict examples, comparative reward-dispersion and learning curves, and tau/beta sensitivity analysis (Figs. 1, 2, 6 and Table 6). It reworks the stage ablations into two- and three-component comparisons. Bias analyses are retained in reduced form, while v1's 1,000-video prompt-strictness experiment and extended qualitative cases are not included. Additional order and sensitivity-curve analyses referenced by v2 cannot be inspected.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seed counts, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. v2's new reward-standard-deviation curves describe within-group reward dispersion, rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Wan-1.3B VBench results change: the Qwen-72B total becomes 80.56 from 80.22, and Qwen-7B becomes 79.90 from 79.67. These accompany the changed training budget and are not controlled same-setting gains. v2 also adds evaluator configurations, revised ablation entries, sensitivity results, human preferences, and comparative training trends. The Wan-14B/Qwen-72B and Hunyuan benchmark values are retained.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the mathematical interpretation of Hoyer sparsity: low values indicate compressed scores, whereas v1 incorrectly associates high values with similar scores. It also revises the component-utility definition and supplies its terminal boundary condition. No theorem or proof development is added.

C1.justification: The principal contribution shifts from a competence-driven, co-evolving reward curriculum to a Goodhart-based diagnosis of shortcut optimization and lost within-group discrimination, addressed by TaRoS. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion foreground robust reward signaling and saturated-component suppression. Broad claims of improved visual, motion, and semantic quality remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the mechanism interpretation around shortcut directions, noisy advantages, saturation, and training collapse. It argues that evaluator scaling alone is insufficient and adds a rationale for prioritizing visual fidelity. Section 5.5 explicitly acknowledges that the method mitigates rather than completely eliminates reward hacking, qualifying the stronger prevention language in its abstract.

D1.justification: Available reproducibility documentation contracts substantially. v1 Appendix A and Fig. 14 provide batch and accumulation settings, optimizer and SDE details, threshold calibration, and exact reward prompts; v2 refers these matters to supplementary material absent from the supplied PDF. v2 newly discloses reward normalization to [0,10] and a smoothing window of 50. This concerns available documentation, not proof that omitted implementation settings changed.

R1.justification: Research positioning moves from curriculum and cognitive-learning inspiration toward Goodhart's law and multi-objective reward optimization. v2 adds relevant reinforcement-learning, InstructVideo, and gradient-manipulation references while dropping several earlier curriculum and neuroscience citations. It also newly contrasts its approach with rigid stage schedules and memory-intensive gradient methods.

P1.justification: The title, method terminology, abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 adds a Discussion section, consolidates benchmark interpretation, moves qualitative analysis before ablations, and relocates the coefficient-of-variation explanation. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to a single-column layout. v2 redraws the pipeline, replaces introductory illustrations, splits the combined Wan table, transposes the Hunyuan table, and combines real/generated bias plots with fewer comparator traces. New diagnostic plots and human-evaluation/sensitivity tables further change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the evidence through matched-evaluator controls, sensitivity tests, and human ratings, and corrects the Hoyer-index explanation. However, exact reward prompts, threshold calibration, and extensive training details available in v1 are missing from the supplied v2, which instead cites unavailable supplementary material. These gains and substantial reproducibility gaps prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement from the supplied PDFs.
